title: What stories can two expressions with letters tell?
description: Two expressions with letters are given with no story, and the video makes up a shop story and a factory story for them. Each story is checked with numbers in place of the letters.
teaching_notes: One idea: a number of items times a price or a rate, joined by plus or minus, gives a story for an expression. Watch for students who give a story in which the two amounts cannot be added or taken away from each other.

video_script.why: A learner uses the method of the bill expression in the other direction: each part is a number of items times the price of one item, and the plus or minus joins the amounts.
video_script.substitution: The method of the bill expression run backwards, from the expression to a story.
video_script.anchor: two expressions with letters that need a story
video_script.payoff_line: Many other situations fit these expressions

final_answer.value: Many other situations fit; model: 8 pens at x rupees and 3 notebooks at y rupees; 15 chairs made on each of j days, 2 spoiled on each of k days
final_answer.spoken: many other situations fit, for example eight pens at x rupees with three notebooks at y rupees, and fifteen chairs made on each of j days with two spoiled on each of k days

never_show: the statement that many other situations fit, before the answer beat
maths_rules: 8 × x + 3 × y: 8 pens at x rupees each and 3 notebooks at y rupees each.
15 × j − 2 × k: 15 chairs made on each of j days, and 2 chairs spoiled on each of k days.
video_script.design: One idea: an expression is read backwards into a story, with a count times a price or rate for each part. Assumes the bill expression. The two expressions stay on the stage and each story is drawn beside them. No wrong idea is raised.

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>In a bill, the number of items is multiplied by the price of one item.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>The amounts of different items are then added together.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>A letter can stand for a price, or for a number of days.

narration: <bookmark mark='s1a'/>Let x be the price of one pen and y the price of one notebook, in rupees.
<bookmark mark='s1b'/>A shopper buys eight pens and three notebooks. The pens cost eight times x.
<bookmark mark='s1c'/>The notebooks cost three times y, and the total cost is the two amounts added.

narration: <bookmark mark='s2a'/>A factory makes fifteen chairs on each of j days, which is fifteen times j chairs.
<bookmark mark='s2b'/>On each of k days, two chairs are spoiled, which is two times k chairs.
<bookmark mark='s2c'/>The good chairs left are the chairs made, take away the chairs spoiled.

marks.s3a: 10 and 20 are put in place of x and y in the shop story
marks.s3b: 2 and 1 are put in place of j and k in the factory story

narration: <bookmark mark='s3a'/>Check the shop story with x as ten and y as twenty rupees.
<bookmark mark='s3c'/>The pens cost eighty and the notebooks cost sixty, so the total is one hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='s3b'/>Check the factory with j as two and k as one.
<bookmark mark='s3d'/>Thirty chairs are made and two are spoiled, which leaves twenty eight.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Many other situations fit these expressions.
A shop story and a factory story are two of them. You can make up your own.
